jsonld.appDescription: Calculates the annual cost of a repetitive manual task (hours × people × hourly cost) for an SMB.

faq.q: How do you calculate the cost of a manual task in an SMB?
faq.a: Multiply the hours spent per week by the number of people doing it, by the loaded hourly cost (wages + payroll costs), then by 50 weeks. Example: 8 hours × 1 person × $25/h × 50 weeks = $10,000 per year, for a single task.

faq.q: Which hourly cost should I use in the calculation?
faq.a: The “loaded” cost: the hourly wage plus payroll taxes and benefits, roughly 1.2 to 1.4 times the gross wage. For an employee paid $20/h, count $24 to $28/h in real cost.

faq.q: At what amount is automation worth it?
faq.a: Simple rule: if the task costs more per year than the project that eliminates it, it pays for itself in under twelve months. An automation sprint starts at $4,500; a task costing $10,000/year pays it back in about six months. Below that threshold, doing nothing is often the better call — and I’ll tell you so.

steps.title: Under $4,500 a year
steps.text: Automating probably isn’t worth it — the project would cost more than the chore. Keep the template and run the numbers again when volume grows.

steps.title: Between $4,500 and $15,000
steps.text: Sprint territory: one chore eliminated in 2 to 3 weeks, fixed scope, fixed price (from $4,500). The project pays for itself within the first year.

steps.title: Above $15,000
steps.text: There are probably several tasks — or an entire system — to rethink. That’s where a phased system replacement fits: each phase delivered and paid back before the next one starts.
